utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are starting late because there was no power in the courtroom. We'll sit until 11.35, take a 30-minute break, and then resume at 12.05 to 1.45. Mr. Nice, I am to say that your motion for a voir dire is denied, and the Chamber will issue a written decision tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphone be turned towards the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, could you turn your microphone towards yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we left off discussing your agenda, and we were dealing with page 846 -- 446, the last digits.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got my agenda, so could you please provide me with a copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understood it that you had it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was here yesterday, but I don't see it here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Binder 17.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you just remind me of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And then we have to find it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's page 100 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We dealt with the question of sanitisation, "asanacija," where it says that each case must be solved and we must know the truth and the clearing up of the terrain. Now, what does it say under the fifth asterisk?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Legal handling with individuals and property left behind," and in brackets, probably "(vehicles.)" "Lawful treatment," it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what does it say next?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we read this out and there was a mistake in the translation at one point. It says: "Remove traces of violence against property/SUZ," which means the Civil Defence staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the job of the SCZ [as interpreted], to remove traces of debris, et cetera, to clear the area?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that could be their task within the frameworks of clearing up the terrain and clearing up the roads, the communication lines, to ensure free passage and secure passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the following page, in line 1, would you read what it says there.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a blotch on the page there where the first word is. There's a little hole there punched in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says "morale" there.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "And honour." If the first word is moral or morale, then it says: "Morale and honour of the Serbian policemen." And then in brackets: "(Responsibility of chiefs, superiors)."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what is the insistence here? How do you explain that note?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's logical from what I quoted. Insistence is made on moral behaviour and honour of the police force and it is also insisted that it is the superiors who are responsible to see that that is carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then in line 2 it says that "criminal offences perpetrated by the police," and then in brackets it says "(Podujevo)." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Criminal offences perpetrated by the police (Podujevo) - violence towards civilians." Yes. We're quite obviously dealing with the killing that took place in Podujevo, and we've discussed that several times now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, under number 2 --

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it doesn't mean that the police should do this. It is a negative example of what can happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Under number 2, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under number 2, it says: "Crime prevention and the prevention of violence and anarchy," and then it says: "Legality."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says "Legality" in the next line, doesn't it? The next line down.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the next line down but that same sentence, if I understand that correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say under that? Finding what?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Finding the perpetrators of murders, looting, rapes."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Particularly members of the police." And what is meant there is if the police are perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what does it say under that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Detention."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, does this refer to detention for all those who have perpetrated crimes, including the police?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Quite obviously that is what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what it says towards the end of point 2, where it says: "Responsibility for civil conflict must not fall on the police." What's that about?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that the police must take all necessary measures to prevent any conflicts between the citizens, because the police, in conformity with the law, is responsibility for law and order, the freedom of movement, and so on and so forth. So this is emphasised. The role of the police is emphasised in preventing any civil unrest and any other problems for which the police is in charge and for which it is responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, turn over the page and we'll just look at a few of the notes you have there on the next page, on the next piece of paper. And it is point 4: "Organisational matters."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Organisational matters," in the plural.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, organisational matters. That's right. Does it say here: "All units subordinated to the chief -- the SUP chiefs"? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is that in keeping with the explanation you gave as to how the units work; that is to say that the chiefs of the Secretariat of the Interior are the individuals to whom the units are subordinated?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is in conformity with the explanations I gave earlier on and the system of leading the police, managing the police, which remain the same, essentially wasn't changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what does it say, this "OPT under particular control"? What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is OPG.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, OPG.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are operative police groups, OPG, and they should be placed under special control here, as it says, or particular control, as it says here, from the secretariat level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what do we have in brackets there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that is "Djakovica." Probably we had some complaints coming from that region or, rather, from the SUP of Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then what does it say in the next line, the next note?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the next note, it says: "Disciplinary proceedings as per decree." So there was a separate wartime degree which related to disciplinary proceedings, or procedure, and that question was regulated by decree under a different name, a different title, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But insistence is made that the decree is acted upon when it comes to disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And there were some extended competencies for the leaders with respect to the disciplinary accountability of policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's skip the next part where it says control vehicles, et cetera. That's not relevant here. But what does it say next, after that? From your what?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "From your PJP organise super supervisory organs for legality in procedure." Yesterday, in response to a question, I think I said something about that, when the platoon was mentioned. A platoon was mentioned yesterday, and at one point in time we insisted that apart from the leaders and chiefs who in regular procedure are duty-bound to control legality, here we insisted upon the fact that in each of the PJPs there should be a super supervisory body to effect additional control over the legality and police procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that in the unit, does it not, that this high-level control was organised to see that legality was implemented and the chiefs in question were duty-bound to see that the police worked according to the proper rules and the whole hierarchy, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I really must -- I'm not going to bother to protest. I must observe that this was an exhibit produced by the accused. He took the witness to a very limited number of entries in examination-in-chief, and although I could have raised all sorts of points if I had unlimited time, I took him to only a limited number of points in cross-examination, and we're now being taken through the document for an interpretation that I don't necessarily accept, and that's going to have to be the subject of argument in due course on the basis of matters that were only ever explored by one side in re-examination. Whether this is of any value to the Chamber is a matter that the Chamber must decide, but it's taking a great deal of our time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the accused's pointed is that this goes to the question of legality, the culture of proper conduct in the police, Article 7(3) matters, and I think it does arise from your cross-examination, Mr. Nice. But the question is very leading. The question that you asked, Mr. Milosevic, which is that: "That means in the unit ... that this high-level control was organised to see that legality was implemented ..." and as you well know, questions like that are not permissible. They are of a very leading nature. So reformulate the question. Your pattern, as I see it, should be to direct the witness's attention to a particular sentence or item and ask him what it means. Mr. Nice has raised the question as to the value of it, the value of the witness giving his interpretation of it now, and that will go to the weight which the Chamber attaches to evidence on this agenda. And as I raised with you yesterday, Mr. Milosevic, you may consider that you have done as much as you can in relation to this agenda. You have spent a lot of time on it in re-examination, and if you have other matters to deal with, you may consider that your time would be better spent on those matters. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Now, as far as this question goes, the witness quoted what it says on this particular page of the agenda. He read out a sentence which reads as follows: "From your PJP organise super supervisory organs for legality in procedure."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll just stop you. Just ask the witness -- I'll ask him. Yes. Just ask him what it means and don't tell him. Don't formulate a question which tells him the answer. That's the objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what does "Organise super supervisory organs" mean that is mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That simply means that in addition to the leadership cadre in each of the police units, which, according to general provisions, are duty-bound to effect control in addition to all their other assignments, here what is being determined is or, rather, an assignment is being issued to establish in each PJP a separate organ or body for controlling the legality of police procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who else was responsible for legality in proceedings or procedural conduct? Here you call them super supervisory organs. That's what it says here, but who in the regular line of duty is responsible for legality?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said along the regular line of duty, based on regular police regulations, it is the leaders of each of the units that is responsible, and in the ministry there's a separate body for internal control of legality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this body for the internal control of legality that you mentioned just now, is that a permanent body in the ministry or was it just set up ad hoc for the war situation?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a permanent body, and as far as I remember, it was a sector or department for the control of legality or supervision of legality which existed at one point as an independent body or unit within the ministry and at one time it was under the individual administrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the duty of those internal bodies for internal control in the ministry?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is the duty of those bodies first and foremost to control the legality and the conduct of each police unit, and specifically to act upon any complaints that might come in from citizens with respect to any behavioural conduct on the part of any individual policeman or a police unit as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So can we say that it is a police force within the police, controlling the work of the police?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we could put it that way, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, on the right-hand side of this same page you have a note where it says: "Protection from propaganda -- against propaganda." The last sentence on that page.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. It says: "Protection against propaganda."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then it says the army is fighting and the police are stealing. "The VJ is waging war and the police are stealing?" What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I answered this question in Belgrade, so I can remember what it means, but I had to give it some thought. This text was written -- was copied out from a slogan that was a pamphlet and leaflet that was sent out by NATO to effect a rift between the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, could you help me out now. I found it somewhere in your agenda but I'm not able to find it now. You did write down the wording of a leaflet, of a pamphlet that the KLA handed out, calling upon people to leave Kosovo and Metohija. Could you find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Unless it is described in those terms as the wording of a pamphlet, then that would be a clearly leading question. Maybe it is described as a leaflet. We'll have to find out and see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's find out. How was it described? I'm asking Mr. Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to find it. As far as I can remember, in this notebook of mine there is a translation of the text on that leaflet. I wrote it down while somebody was translating it for me over the telephone from the place where it had been found. Will you allow me to find it, please? It's not easy for me to find it, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, as quickly as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, can I place on the overhead projector yet another leaflet which had already been presented here. In all fairness, this is a rather murky photocopy because the original leaflet is red, so the photocopy is dark. The translation is written in hand, and the translation into English is there too. Exhibit D1. You can take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it, if it matters. R017240. 01724240 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... what it says. The point was whether you wrote down the wording of a leaflet, of a pamphlet to the effect that the KLA handed out, calling up on people to leave Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see, it doesn't say that it's a leaflet, but I know that it's a translation of a leaflet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what does it say there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What does it say? What is it that you have written down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the page number again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 0172420.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would be about page 80, I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Page 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Roughly, I'm guessing, from other references. If the witness can give us the first line of what he's reading then we can track it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the first line, Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Brothers and sisters." That's the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 73.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. Page 73, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, could you please read out what you wrote here.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Brothers and sisters, Albanians, NATO has started -" probably - "a war against Serbia." Now, there's something that's in very small letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "That you've waited for for a long time," if I can read it.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see the other -- the second word, rather, perhaps: "Which we have been waiting for for a long time." Then the following asterisk: "The Serbs, out of despair, will embark on despair" [as interpreted] . The fourth asterisk: "The KLA is -" probably - "unable to protect us -" probably - "and NATO --" I cannot read the last word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can read it, it says "far away."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "The KLA is unable to protect us and NATO is far away."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that could be it, roughly. Now I'm having some difficulty in reading the rest. "Take your personal belongings and set out on foot -" probably - "in large groups -" probably "groups" - "towards Macedonia and -" probably - "Albania." And the last point: "That is the only way for us to survive and for NATO --" I can't read the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, the question is where does this come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already explained,

utterances.speaker: MR. PRESIDENT
utterances.text: I jotted this down as somebody telephoned the staff and said that they have a leaflet from the KLA. I immediately asked for them to translate the leaflet for me. They found someone who knew Albanian, and I just jotted down the translation and -- in order to be able to call the minister to inform him about the content of the leaflet. I saw the leaflet later. I think it was pink or red or something like that. I previously quoted the NATO leaflet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask an interpretation question. I see that part of that was interpreted as "In despair, the Serbs will embark on despair," which is not what it says in the leaflet.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that in the translation it says "illegible" whereas the witness said "in despair," and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's have an answer from the interpreter before you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... concerned about is the second use of the word "despair." That's not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The second word was "revenge." Maybe it will be corrected in the LiveNote, but the second word that is actually written there and was said is "revenge."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I return to the observation which is now an objection about the question, which is entirely leading in form as to what this was. Not at all something that the Prosecution necessarily accepts, there being entirely alternative interpretation, and how does this arise under the justification that Your Honours referred to for exploring this book in detail at this stage. This whole line of re-examination is going to prove problematic. I shall draw your attention in another way to the problems of one of the particular entries that has been dealt with by this witness because it touches on a matter of evidence that you're, I think, short of so I'll deal with it in another way. But this last question and answer doesn't seem to relate to the earlier topic at all. It's different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite so. I'll ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this matter is different from the general subject area that you have been dealing with in your re-examination, that's the culture of legality and propriety of conduct on the part of the police. Tell us how this arises from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It arises in view of the assertions made by Mr. Nice that the Serb forces, as he said, expelled Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija. As a matter of fact, he explained to General Stevanovic that General Stevanovic had to know that, that the Serb forces were expelling Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija. Here we can see a leaflet of the KLA calling upon the Albanians to set out on foot in large groups towards Macedonia and Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice, Judge Kwon has reminded us that you examined on similar questions, page 94 in English, at the top, "Results of the operations - last remaining large groups broken up - about 2.000 liquidated - left the country - 900.000 - terrorists remaining ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely right. I cross-examined on the basis that his notebook appeared to say that 900.000 people had left the country, with 2.000 having been liquidated and with 300.000 remaining. Absolutely right. But how does that let in, I ask rhetorically, an alleged reference to a pamphlet when indeed the whole business of pamphlets is controversial, as the Court will remember from the evidence of Rugova who explained the -- his position on similar documents that were put -- or documents of an allegedly similar type put to him and gave his explanation for why it simply wasn't possible for such leaflets to be distributed in the way that was suggested to him. This is a controversial issue and it has to do with propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But the pamphlet suggests that the KLA told people to take their personal belongings and head on foot in large groups towards Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it was a pamphlet. The advice included that the accused led with the suggestion it was a pamphlet. He didn't ask for entry and ask what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very briefly, if I may say the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. following: First of all, the issue of leading questions is one thing which Your Honours are dealing with. The second point that arises specifically in relation to this document is that it's correct that Mr. Nice cross-examined on issues relating and touching upon deportation and forcible transfer, those being two of the counts in the Kosovo indictment; and if you leave aside the issue for the moment of the leading question, surely as a matter of principle, first of all, Mr. Milosevic is entitled to draw to the attention of this witness passages from the diary and ask him what it means - he wrote it - and what it is. And he is also entitled to explain what that document was, and it's then information before the Trial Chamber as to what was allegedly out there and available and possibly being given out - who knows - to individuals in Kosovo at the time. It's circumstantial background evidence that this witness can speak to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But does it arise? But does it arise?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Does it arise out of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes, it arises because Mr. Nice has dealt with issues concerning the numbers of people who were leaving Kosovo, and it arises as a subissue out of that as to possibly why people were leaving or what was out there at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber finds that the issue arises from cross-examination, but, Mr. Milosevic, don't exhaust us on this matter. When do you -- when will your re-examination be concluded? It should be today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As soon as I can do it, but, Mr. Robinson, please bear in mind that Mr. Nice, in cross-examination, did start an entire spectrum of subjects that were not the subject of examination-in-chief at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've already ruled, so proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. I believe that you have made the right ruling, because this is truly relevant. It's a question of why they actually left Kosovo. Before I proceed, I wish to react to what Mr. Nice said a few moments ago, that their witness, or his witness, challenged something. May I remind you that yesterday when we were discussing the question of Izbica, he said that their witnesses spoke otherwise, as if what their witnesses were saying was true. In relation to that, for example, in relation to Izbica, and he referred to their witnesses, I wish to remind you and Mr. Kwon, who did listen to their witnesses at the time, that that witness from Izbica, like a few other witnesses from Izbica, that these were witnesses who cannot have any kind of credibility whatsoever. For example, may I remind that you on page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this is not the moment of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is not the moment for comment like that. Let us move on with the re-examination and try to conclude it as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Izbica was a subject of cross-examination by Mr. Nice. My associates looked up these witnesses that Mr. Nice referred to. Milazim Thaci testified, for example, with regard to Izbica, and you have an exhibit there which is a photograph of a shirt with holes, and he said that he was shot, executed with a heavy machine-gun, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is how we consume time needlessly. Let us proceed with the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, not on this matter, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only just -- yes, but to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If no, simply to draw to your attention that the accused has, as a matter of fact, served as his tab 437 a Prosecution partial analysis of the diary, and if you're interested in seeing it and if that becomes an exhibit, the very point that we've been dealt with is dealt with at paragraph 28 of that document because he chose to put in the Prosecution's analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, to continue with your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at that leaflet which you have before you on the ELMO, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the leaflet please be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The leaflet is available in its original form. It is printed on the red paper. However, we also have a photocopy provided by the Registry. Would you please put the photocopy on the ELMO. I can't see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the one that can be seen only in the courtroom, but the one that is broadcast to the public does not show this leaflet. Can you see the KLA symbol in the upper part of the page?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the leaflet is in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The leaflet is printed on red paper. You have it in the records. Would you please read out the translation, the translation in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it, other than what was read out to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. You have it on the next page. You have the translation into Serbian. Can you see the Serbian translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who provided that translation, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those who found the leaflet. Somebody out there in the field who found the leaflet translated it right there on the spot, under the existing conditions, wrote down the translation in handwriting and then sent it further up the chain. You also have the translation into English, and I assume that somebody verified it and compared it both with the Albanian text and the Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you read out the translation?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, although this is not in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I never said it was in your handwriting. I just said that this is a similar type of leaflet. I never indicated that it was in your handwriting.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Therefore, we here -- or, rather: "Distinguished fellow citizens. We are hereby informing you to evacuate yourselves from the territories of the Republic of Kosovo which are threatened, because in the continuation of combat, the large offensive of the Serb occupying forces in our Republic of Kosovo is continued. We cannot defend you. This cannot be done by the KLA either. "I have -- we have to save our people and their lives. Therefore, set out immediately in the direction of Albania and Macedonia. We have asked from NATO to halt the Serb occupiers. With that assistance, we have won. However, the forces, the forces," yes, I think it says, "the forces of the Serb occupiers are in the entire territory of Kosovo. They have launched a large offensive. The KLA forces are unable to put up resistance and defend the Siptar nation. We are hereby informing all Siptars who are exposed to danger at the hands of the Serb occupiers to evacuate themselves first and foremost in the direction of Macedonia and Albania. "The President of the Republic of Kosovo, Ibrahim Rugova." This is the text of this translation written in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So one translation was dictated to you over the phone. This is another leaflet. General, based on your stay in Kosovo, do you know that there were a number of such leaflets urging Albanians to move out from Kosovo and go to Albania or Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a number of leaflets were dropped. I didn't know, though, that the contents were different. The contents of the leaflet that was dictated to me on the phone is similar to this one but not identical with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody's claiming that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're again asking leading questions. The fact that the Prosecutor has not objected or that the point has not been taken doesn't mean that when the Chamber comes to assess the weight it will not take account of the fact that the answer resulted from an impermissible form of questioning. An answer which comes from a leading question is relatively worthless. This is an important area of the case and you must be careful, you must be circumspect in the way questions are phrased. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, did you hear that there were such leaflets urging them to do this or did you hear of just one such leaflet that -- the translation of which was dictated to you on the phone?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote down the translation of one leaflet which was translated to me on the phone. However, I heard about a number of leaflets that were dropped in Pristina and some other towns. I thought that all those leaflets were identical, the same. However, based on this translation, it seems that there were a number of such leaflets with different text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, please, let's take a look at the next page, 449. Please take a look at your agenda. 449 are the last three digits of the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say here, to focus on the following tasks, look under 1 and 2. What does it say under 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under 1, it says: "Anti-terrorist operations," and 2 is: "Prevention of crime and anarchy."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What can we see under this point: "Prevention of crime," and so on?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Prevention of crime and anarchy." And then underneath, it says: "Solving grave crimes - murders - lootings," and then underneath, it says: "Finding and confiscating most likely stolen items."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Stolen items. Very well. Let's go to the following page. What does it say on the right-hand side, 450 are the last three digits. It says: "Problems."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, under item 6, it says: "Problems," and then underneath: "3.600 detained."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened to those 3.600 people who were detained? How many were kept in detention and how many were released? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, such detentions of a large number of people were generally brief. After the typical procedure, as a rule, majority of those were released and only those who were suspected of belonging to the terrorist organisations or having committed some crimes were kept in detention. In the continuation, if this is needed, it says "Turning terrorists into civilians." This is an issue that we have mentioned several times here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you remember, General, what this is actually about? The circumstances in which 3.600 people were detained, or is it a proposal to detain 3.600 people, or is it over a period of time, or is it on one day, or what's it all about? I'm finding this just a tedious exercise in going through notes that you can't actually tell us very much in detail about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally I can't go into detail regarding each entry, but I can tell you something more about this notation that 3.600 people were detained. Most likely this has to do with a total number of people detained from the beginning of the war until this date. I don't know what was this date. And that -- this was a large problem for police, namely to investigate all of these detainees and decide who needs to be released and who needs to be detained further, because the heading above it indicates problems. This is an unusually large number of detained persons, and the resources of police in Kosovo were not so great to be able to process all of this in the -- within the time deadline specified in law. Those who were detained were suspected of having ties to terrorist organisation. However, the majority were released soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you think this is the total number who were detained between the 24th of March and the 7th or 8th of May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already explained that these were people regarding whom there were reasonable grounds to believe that they either belonged to terrorist organisations or participated in terrorist acts. And this probably does not reflect the situation on that date but probably reflects the total number of persons detained from the beginning of the war. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that says -- your last three words say it all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As I indicated yesterday, the Chamber will have to give very careful consideration to the weight to be attached to the evidence that has been adduced through this witness both in examination-in-chief and in cross-examination and also in re-examination. In some cases the witness is fairly certain as to the meaning of entries in this diary, or agenda as he calls it. In other cases, his answers amount to nothing more than a mere conjecture, a mere surmise. But it is a matter that the Trial Chamber will have to address, as I said, very carefully. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, I cannot find in your agenda a similar entry, but I believe that I saw somewhere in your agenda an entry reflecting the number of persons detained and then kept in detention. Can you find that? I think that I remember seeing something along the lines 1.000 or so detained and about 200 kept in detention.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there must be such an entry in the agenda, but I -- it wouldn't be easy for me to find it. But I think it's stated taken into custody and detained. And the difference is great, because normally you take into custody a large number of people but then you keep in detention only a small number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. At the bottom of the page there is the word "Judicial system." Is that also something that falls under this category, under the heading "Problems"?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says there "Judicial system," and probably has to do with the relations between the police and the judicial system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And then the following heading is "The movement of civilians." Can you find that?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says here: "Movements of civilians." This is the last asterisk on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And below that it says something: "Across the border or not across the border," and then it says "200.000." What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained this yesterday. This was the constant dilemma that we had as to what should be done with the people who wanted to cross the border. Should we apply the force and prevent them or should we let them go? Either option was difficult, in a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, could you read the number again after "Over or across the border." Is it not 800.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could be 800.000, although at first glance it looks as 200.000. But it could be 800.000, because as I told you before, I seem to remember that figure, and I think that this was towards the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Another example of the dangers of leading, and Your Honour made the observation that I don't always take the point. If I took every point, I'd hardly be on my seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice. May I ask the general, you have called this document an agenda as distinct from a diary. What is the distinction that you make between an agenda and a diary? This may be relevant to the question of how this document is to be viewed by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would say that the best name for this document would be a notebook. It's not a diary. Definitely not a diary, because "diary" means noting down the events, what was going on, whereas this document obviously does not do that. These are my personal notes. And if you go through this carefully, you will see it for yourself. You can find here the words of -- uttered by other people, the words that I planned to utter myself at a meeting. You can find the text of a NATO leaflet here or a KLA leaflet. So the contents are diverse and written down in abbreviated form which was clear only to me at that particular time, and this is what is problematic in a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Isn't that the distinction, that in this notebook or agenda the format is abbreviated, and in a diary it would not be so abbreviated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that would be the vital difference. A diary should be a description of what actually happened, or a description of how I see what happened, my opinions of something that happened. So a diary is a description of events and things that happened in one's life, in the course of one's job, and so on. That's how I understand the term "diary." Whereas here you can see that they are notes. Some notes refer to the future, what is planned in the future, what I want to say somewhere or what somebody said at one point in time, what somebody told me, what somebody conveyed to me over the telephone and asked me to pass the message on to someone else. So it's very difficult for me now to remember all the details of my notes. I remember what I thought very well and that those notes that I jotted down and that are part of the terminology and words that I use. It is difficult for me to remember what other people said and that I took note of and why it was put in that way and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on. General, would you turn to page 451, the ERN number has the last digits 451.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And could you explain to us what it says there.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where, on the left or right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 451 left, left-hand side. Or left and right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, before we move off, I would like to hear the explanation on the next line after "800.000." There it says: "Still 3.000 - 400.000." Could you explain that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite certainly this refers to the number of those citizens who remained in Kosovo and Metohija. That is quite obvious. That's the assessment, the estimate. The number of citizens who did not leave Kosovo and Metohija during that period of time when that note was written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, I asked you to turn to page 451, the ERN number, and could you explain to us what it says there.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us find it in the English. It's the very next page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it's the very next page but somewhere there. Let me just take a look. Yes, the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I explained in detail what this means in response to a question from the Prosecutor. Of course, I can repeat it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we dealing with "No corpse, no crime"? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that what you're dealing with, "No corpse, no crime"? We have been through that already, so you can --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what comes next here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes. Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, could you please explain to us what it says here.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we have a note -- here we have a note of a statement by the representative of either the state security service or the public -- military security about a meeting on the perfidiousness in the work of the KLA terrorists. The first thesis says: "No corpse, no crime." And in crime that is a well-known thesis, a philosophy, a manner of thinking, that is to say what criminals do when there is a death, that is to cover up the bodies, to cover up the corpse to avoid crime or responsibility and accountability for a crime. In the second point, the second thesis is that that is done, and the word "mucki" is used.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We explained what that means; perfidious, treacherous, in the Serbian language perhaps worse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is much worse than the word "perfidious," and it can only refer to somebody who is your enemy. According to the third thesis as written here, it is stated: "They will justify the aggression using evidence of crimes." So that is an assessment made by persons from the security organs, and their operative knowledge indicates that they will make scenes which will allegedly prove certain crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So in -- with that background, can you explain the reference to "No corpse, no crime"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. That sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't repeat. If you want to use evidence of crimes to justify aggression, you need the corpses. What I'm trying to understand is the reference to "No corpse, no crime" in the context in which you've just described the three separate lines here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've explained that, too, Your Honour. Allow me to repeat it in a different way perhaps, explain it in another way. I've already said that they are getting rid of the bodies from the police, removing them from the police, the police who is going to come in and prove a crime, and then they group them and collect them together in mass graves later on, which they want to show as being the consequence of crimes committed by Serb forces, and in that context I wanted to explain the existence of this alleged mass grave in Pusto Selo. When we learnt of that grave site, then we remembered the story and what was said at that meeting about all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I have to say at first sight that's a very imaginative reading of what's here. There's no reference to mass graves, burying bodies, or anything of that nature. What's referred to is obliterating the evidence of crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't agree, of course, because I know exactly what the subject was and what was said about it at the time. Of course, I just jotted down certain theses and guidelines for myself so that I could have a proper understanding of the problem in hand, because Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this wasn't aimed at explaining this to anybody else. All I did was to note it down for myself, what I understood it to mean in the way that I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, you began your answer to the question put by the accused by saying that this is a note of a statement by the representative of either the state security service or military security about a meeting on the perfidiousness, something, but we note on the right side the words "The president." Is this not the word of the president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, obviously I wasn't precise enough, or the interpretation was not the right one. I said clearly this is my note about what other people said, what somebody said, one of the representatives of one or the other service at a meeting held in the president's place. So some -- my note was that somebody had said -- a representative of the security services said it and it was stated at the meeting at the president's place. I think that makes it clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you need to consider this: It is not every point that is raised in cross-examination that you should re-examine on. You must be selective as to the points, and you need only re-examine on a point where you think your case has been challenged and you need to rehabilitate the witness, or you may end up prejudicing your case. My recollection on this particular passage is that we had a translation which was in your favour. Why are you reopening it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me be very direct on this point, Mr. Robinson -- but let me just ask a question before I do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in the explanations we have just heard by Mr. Bonomy, covering up the bodies and so on, the corpses, how does this second thesis that you jotted down, how is that incorporated and can be fitted into what he said? Because you have jotted down different questions raised by individuals. This, in the B/C/S interpreter's note, it is "mucki rad." So how does that thesis fall into what Mr. Bonomy said?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for somebody to use his own -- for his own work, an adjective of that kind is very difficult to explain because it was used as a very low, nasty word that word was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what does it say as the one but last thesis? It says: "We will work --" what does it say? I don't know what it says here. "When the mission arrives, it will be more difficult --" "When the mission arrives, it will be more difficult for us." We can see that.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what mission could this refer to in Kosovo in general terms during those years? What does the word "mission" there imply?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember any other meaning of that word except for the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Now, on this piece of paper there is no date.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this: The mission is mentioned, a mission that is supposed to arrive, due to arrive.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's something I thought about, and I already said that, I think. This sentence could not be written after that date. It would have to be -- or, rather, that meeting would have to have been held before the arrival of the Verification Mission, that is to say in the course of 1998. So that's the problem that I highlighted when I explained all the problems relating to this particular entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, let me answer you, Mr. Robinson. I had to take the witness back to this point because the manner in which Mr. Nice presented this entire entry or note led to what he wished it to lead to, produced what he wished, that is to say that in the media we should hear assertions that in the diary, as they call this, the diary of General Stevanovic, there was an entry that I ordered corpses to be removed from Kosovo. So it was only on the basis of this particular note, this entry that he wrote down there, these theses that he pinpointed, where the term used was "mucki rad," perfidious work of those who worked perfidiously, which was common knowledge. And that is why I claim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will continue, but that is why I claim that Mr. Nice aims at sensationalism and not this trial, and that will be proved correct in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am obliged to rise on this occasion to make two points. The interpretation "mucki rad" will be the subject of a report from the CLSS, and by no means is it accepted that it has a single and simple interpretation. It was, after all, the original words read out by and originally interpreted by the witness in the form of "back-breaking" that we heard. The Court will also have in mind in light of the last observation by both the accused in conjunction with the witness that page 106 - and the pages reflect pages in the book - begins with numbers 7 and 8, and the Chamber will have in mind the observations on timing the witness has himself made about item number 6 on the previous page. The suggestion that I am doing other than my best to conduct a careful analysis of material of this kind that comes before us is entirely rejected and inappropriate. I put my case, and I don't for one minute resile from a sentence of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Nice. Let's proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have to object to what Mr. Nice has just said, that is to say the witness never said -- used the word "mucan." It says in the Serbian language here "mucki rad." Now, the fact that Mr. Nice doesn't know Serbian is not his fault, of course, no fault of his own, but I who know the Serbian language very well know full well that "mucki rad" cannot have more explanations or more meanings, as Mr. Nice claims. And regardless of what any of his interpreters or translators would say, there are 10 million Serbs listening and everybody knows what "mucki rad" means, and everybody knows that "mucki rad" means nothing else but something underhand, something low and underhand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Milosevic. We have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, can I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I haven't been yet accused by Mr. Nice of not knowing the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you this: The entry that we are considering is on the same page as the preceding entries with the numbers 7 and 8, and they seem to follow on from the page before that with the number 6. Now, in the light of that, do you still maintain that the entry we've been looking at relates to 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I maintain that only by the use of the word "mission," because really there is no other mission or anything else that that term would use to explain any other concept, any other mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When, then, do you think that the entries number 6, 7, and 8 which span these two pages were written?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from replacing the staff, it was done in six months. So the 8 is a relative figure. We can't use that to claim anything, "8. Replacing the staff." And number 7, "The terrorists now," that doesn't mean much just taken by itself. Now, 6, "Problems," that should relate, in my opinion, to the wartime period. The numbers, of course, I can't say anything about that. It was slightly higher during the war. It says 16.000 as a maximum number here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do these -- do these -- obviously numbers 7 and 8 are on a different page from number 6, but do they look as though they are consecutive pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how it would appear, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So taking up that question by my colleague, the last item on that part in B/C/S, top right, there's a number, 3.600. I think that's the identical number which we saw on the previous page, which refers to the number of persons detained. I think that this is a breakdown of that number. Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally think that this just happens to be a coincidence. I assume that this number, 3.600, on the next page refers to the number of personnel in the unit. Kuci, 500, for instance; 5 times 100. So I cannot see from this information that that has anything to do with the number of detained persons. But indeed it is the same number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. What does it mean "500 home," then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe to return home at that time, but I cannot identify what the rest means, "5 times 100," because 5 times 100 -- or 500. And I can't read the word after that at all. "KP" can only mean Kosovo Polje, but I'm not sure about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, 455 is the page.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's the 21st of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand side you have "asanacija, sanitisation, 1," and the second one is "Crimes, crimes - resolving."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And "KP Dom Istok" is a note that you have further on on the right-hand side. What does it say there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say. Ah, yes. The second point is: "0830 KPD Istok."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "11 projectiles," probably. There is no full stop after that. "Assistant warden -" probably - "killed." That corresponds to what I remember as well, Kalicanin or something like that. And then the next point is "997," probably "prisoners," and it is hard for me to read the rest of what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "0930: Unmanned aircraft shot down"?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "unmanned aircraft shot down," but maybe it says "fleeing." I cannot read it. Maybe that's what it means but I have no recollection, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then what does it say, "Mines"?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Humanitarian --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I remember that a team of the UN, of the humanitarian organisations, had a problem with booby-traps, and there were consequences of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any mention of cluster bombs there?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cluster bombs is the last point within that entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what's the next word, which I cannot read?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Emigration."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And underneath, "Serbs"?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Serbs, Albanians."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: One is Serbs, the other is Albanians, the two bullets.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps that actually pertains to emigration. So evacuation perhaps would have been the right word. It probably means departure from Kosovo, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then further on, it says: "Meeting in Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What's the next word, "statistics"?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "Statistics of criminal offences committed and of perpetrators."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So "Statistics of criminal offences committed and of perpetrators." And then underneath that it says "statistics --"

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Refugee statistics."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it has to do with refugee statistics?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and residence statistics, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then "Terrorist attacks," and then it says, "The number of detainees, statistics of cases, terrorists attacks and their consequences."

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Bombing and its consequences," and its practically illegible from there on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Map of deployment," as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these are the tasks, as far as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice, Ms. Higgins, can I ask, is this a reasonable way to approach this agenda? There are two problems: When the entries are not legible, the witness has to decipher and sometimes the question suggests the meaning, suggests -- not the meaning but what is written, and the witness may or may not agree. The second issue is as to the meaning which the witness is -- which the witness gives to the particular item. But in my view, there is generally a problem in deciding how to assess the meaning that the witness gives now to the passage, but that problem is aggravated when the particular item, the particular passage is not clear. And when the particular passage is not clear, I wonder whether he should be asked at all about the meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I go first, I don't think that, beyond the objections I've made already, I could raise specifically an objection that lack of -- or alleged lack of clarity of a passage would automatically bar further questioning about it, not least because the Prosecution's position will be that this is a witness who is not worthy of credit and, therefore, questions of deciphering the passages in the book may not themselves be accurate or honest assertions by him, and accordingly I fear that our position will be that his answers on particular passages of potential relevance will to be seen as a whole. So that it was with that in mind, amongst other reasons, that I restricted the questions I could ask to a very limited number of topics, and on all of those I think he acknowledged the handwriting as clearly his and I don't think he - I may be wrong - but in any of those passages did he raise significant issues of clarity or non-clarity of the written word, but he has done that with other passages since, and eager though I am to bring this -- or hear this re-examination brought to a close, I don't feel I can invite you simply to cut off his answers on that. My arguments about that may include arguments of the kind I've intimated. So I'm sorry I can't be more helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you. Ms. Higgins, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly, as I have addressed the issue before. Concerning this evidence, in my submission it has to be taken evidently, the original, the translation that has been provided, and the evidence that is being given by the witness in the witness box. It's going to be one of those issues, in my submission, that will be -- have to be dealt with in final submissions as to what the Trial Chamber should advisedly take from this evidence, it being ultimately a matter for your discretion and your decision. I'm not sure that I can assist very much further beyond that, Your Honour. There are clearly difficulties which are inherent in any type of document like this. It's clear that the witness has been very specific on some of the entries and has been able to assist. On others, it's less clear. I'm not sure how I can really assist you any further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, since these are personal notes taken by the witness that were written just in abbreviated form as an outline, I think that these personal notes can be interpreted only by the witness. That is an elementary rule. It's not that he was keeping minutes of any kind. He was making personal notes for his own use in terms of what he considered necessary during the course of his work. So he's the one who can interpret these notes. And I think that there are legible sections in these notes, and it can be seen very clearly there is a red thread that goes throughout this notebook, care for, lawfulness, civilians, resolving crimes, moral behaviour on the part of the police, and so on and so forth. That can clearly be identified from one note to the other. And now Mr. Nice's objection to the effect that I have been putting many questions about this notebook, as the witness called it himself, I wish to remind you that it's precisely from Mr. Nice that I received this document in accordance with Rule 68. It was quite clear to them when they gave it to me as exculpatory documentation that it contains notes that clearly indicate that even in his private notes that were not meant for publication of any kind this witness wrote things down the way they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Its disclosure was not on the basis of being wholly or exclusively under Rule 68 from everything that's known about this document and from the way it was raised in questioning with this witness when he was interviewed as a suspect. It's always been, at best, a document that might have had material that could have been interpreted as exculpatory. That was one of reasons for serving it, but it would have been served in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Since this matter has arisen twice, I think it appropriate to indicate at least a preliminary view I have. I think what Mr. Milosevic has submitted just now is very close to the mark of the significance of the document. It is an aide-memoire. It's a notebook, as the witness has explained, and its use may either enhance or indeed undermine the credibility and reliability of the witness's evidence. Beyond that, it may have a separate use as identifying statements made by people which are either consistent with or inconsistent with other evidence and may either support or undermine that evidence. Indeed, the entries could, I suppose, in extreme circumstances also be viewed individually as indicating something. But it seems to me that its primary use is an aide-memoire to the oral evidence being given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take the break now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in one of your previous notations in your agenda, you entered the information concerning the bombing of the Dubrava KP Dom in Istok. I hope you remember that, because we just took a look at it in the previous session. Was that something that was reported to you? Was that information you received?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat my answer. Yes. It is obvious that that was reported to me either from the Pec secretariat or perhaps one of the members of the staff in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at page 457.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the left side, what does it say there under the second asterisk?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the second asterisk, it says, "Istok evacuated," and then underneath, "591 healthy."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean 591?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "591 healthy - 196 wounded (75)" of 70. I'm not quite sure what it is. And then underneath it, the following entry is "Dead." This is what this abbreviation stands for. "80 plus 7 plus 4 equals 91." That's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was the information you received and this is what you noted down regarding Istok.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And now, finally, page 459.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, do you remember what it means, 80 plus 7 plus 4? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. It could imply some kind of a structure; men, women. I'm not quite sure what it means. Or perhaps I received information subsequently, in stages, and I kept adding these figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could it be different locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. It could only imply different stages at which I received information about the newly uncovered bodies or the dead or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, page 459. On the left side under the second asterisk, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "The legality of the decree --" "Legality," and then underneath it says: "Decree, failure to respond to mobilisation, criminal responsibility," and then an abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I have just a few more questions regarding this agenda, General. Please tell us very briefly under what circumstances you made these notations, these notes.

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under very different circumstances; sometimes in meetings, sometimes as I was preparing for meetings, sometimes when somebody called me on the phone and gave me certain information. So the contents of my notes are quite diverse in terms of how I was writing this down. This could reflect my thought, this could reflect somebody else's thoughts, it could be something that I agree with, something that I do not agree with. So different kinds of things are recorded in this notebook, and their origin was quite diverse as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You are very familiar with your own notebook, and I assume that you could answer several questions regarding everything that is entered here. Based on what is entered in your agenda, what can be said about the ethnic structure of Kosovo and Metohija that our state organs and politicians advocated?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be seen in a thesis, in one of the theses, but I know very well that the police of Serbia advocated multi-ethnic structure in Kosovo and Metohija, and in one of the entries it is stated clearly that the ethnic composition of police needs to be improved in certain regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And based on your agenda, what can be seen about the conduct of state organs, police, and the army?

utterances.speaker: OBRAD STEVANOVIC [Resumed]
